text.p: A group of disgruntled Eurotunnel investors said on Wednesday they were unimpressed by a potential extension of the company's licence to run the Channel Tunnel and were determined to derail a crucial refinancing plan.

The French and British governments have agreed to extend Eurotunnel SA /Plc's concession to 99 years if a restructuring of its 70 billion francs ($12 billion) of bank debt is approved and the firm pays 25 percent of net profit after 2052.
But Adacte, a small radical group of mainly French shareholders, says the licence extension does not meet a basic demand, that banks cancel 40 percent of loans to Eurotunnel.

"We think the only way for Eurotunnel to be viable is that the banks abandon part of the debt," Emmanuelle Bobin, spokeswoman for Adacte said. Without a debt write-off, Eurotunnel's debt service problems will be postponed a few years before another debt restructuring.

In any future debt deal, Adacte believes shareholders will be further diluted to a quarter of the capital from the 54.5 percent proposed in the current deal. "They will lose their voice, it will be too late," she said.
Adacte has so far gathered proxy votes for around two million shares and expects to hold proxies for at least 10 million for a shareholders' meeting next week which will vote on the deal.
It believes that, with the help of proxies for institutional investors held by lawyer Sophie L'Helias, the deal can be blocked, forcing bankers to give up some of their loans.
Adacte does not believe executive chairman Patrick Ponsolle's warning that the company will go bankrupt if the deal is rejected. "They will appoint someone else to clean up the mess," Bobin said.
The carrot being dangled by the licence extension failed to provide solace. "If there's a bankruptcy in five years time, we won't see 99 years," she said.

The investor resistance movement suffered a setback on Monday when U.S. fund Northern Cross Investments, which holds three percent of Eurotunnel's stock, instructed L'Helias to vote in favour of the restructuring, reversing its earlier position.

However, that change of heart did not change the view of other investors represented by L'Helias, who will vote against the debt deal. They are calling for 25 percent debt forgiveness and a cancellation of the "substitution clause" which allows banks to take over the Tunnel.

Christian Cambier of the Eurotunnel Shareholders Association, which represents mainly professional class investors, welcomed the licence extension and said the 25 percent profit share for the governments was acceptable.

"The 99 years give a better visibility," he said, adding that it also meant Eurotunnel did not need to put money into reserves to bid for a renewal of its licence when the current concession expires in 2052 as planned.
"Twenty-five percent for the government means 75 for the shareholders," he said. Under the debt deal, all the interest would have been paid off by 2034.
Eurotunnel needs two thirds consent from French shareholders and 75 percent from British investors. The shareholders meeting has been called for July 10. ($ = 5.881 French Francs)
